I have been farming these 5 mu in Quzhou County for 25 years now. I know every corner of this plot, and I know what works here. I am 45 years old, finished junior high, and my household has five mouths to feed. With some of my family working off-farm, labor is tight during the busy seasons, so I cannot afford to waste time or take unnecessary risks.

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October right after the maize came off. I used an improved wheat variety because it gives me stable yields and stands up to our winter cold. I tilled the land with the rotary tiller before sowing to break up the maize stubble and prepare a clean seedbed. Now that spring has arrived, the wheat is greening up. I will topdress nitrogen at jointing and irrigate three times in total: the overwintering irrigation I already did, one at green-up or jointing now, and one more during grain filling in May. Over the whole season I put down about 17 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphorus and potassium from compound fertilizer — roughly 11 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium per mu. I spray pesticides four times to keep weeds, disease, and insects under control. If the weather holds, I expect about 500 kg per mu at harvest in early June.

After the wheat comes off, I have to plant the summer maize fast — the window is short. I will use a hybrid variety, probably Zhengdan 958 or Denghai 605, the kinds the seed shop always stocks and that my neighbors trust. I will not till the soil; I will direct-seed straight into the wheat stubble to save time, save fuel, and keep the moisture in the ground. For the maize I apply about 11 kg nitrogen per mu, side-dressed when the plants are knee-high, plus around 3 kg each of phosphorus and potassium at planting. I irrigate twice — once if June turns dry, and definitely once at tasseling because summer rains cannot be relied on even with my well. Three pesticide sprays handle the weeds and corn borers. I should get about 550 kg per mu from the maize by late September.

This is the way I have always done it. It fits my land, my well, and my household's labor. I do not chase fancy new methods; I stick to what brings in the crop.
